title: Introduction to Version Control and Git
summary: Conceptual intro to version control with Git: commits act as save points of a project that you can compare against or restore. Previews the module: local Git on the command line, then cloning, forking, pull requests and merging.

concepts.heading: Version control as save points
points: Putting a file under version control with Git lets you record snapshots of it over time. Each snapshot is a version (in Git terms a commit), for example version 1 after the first few lines and version 2 after more work.
If later changes wreck the code, you can diff the broken working copy against any earlier snapshot to see what changed, or roll back to a saved version.
You can return to any recorded version, not only the most recent one, as long as you know which one you want.
Rollback matters most when code is interdependent (many files or classes relying on each other), where a bad change can be hard to untangle by hand.

concepts.heading: Module roadmap
points: Git is used from the command line: local version control first (next lesson).
Later topics: GitHub remotes, cloning repositories, branching and merging, forking and pull requests.

pitfalls: (Extra) Git only keeps versions you explicitly commit; unsaved edits between commits cannot be recovered from Git.

gaps_and_ideas: A short interactive 'save points' timeline: the learner edits a file, clicks Commit to add a node, then restores or diffs against an earlier node.
